rubric: DISCRETE MATHEMATICS / THE LANGUAGE OF MATHEMATICS / CHAPTER 1

slides.title: Sets: the language of mathematics
slides.main: A set is the foundation of the whole course: without it you cannot understand relations, counting, or logic.

captions: Elements appear: five circles and five squares
Each group can be circled — we get two sets
Now the shapes have colors: blue, red, green
Let's circle by color — the same shapes, but now three different sets

body.text: Unique values in code, unions and intersections in database queries, a user's set of permissions — you use sets every day.

slides.title: What a set is
slides.sub: Exactly two things: which elements are in it — and which are not
slides.main: An element either belongs to the set or it doesn't — there is no third option.

captions: A set is a collection of elements
Exactly two things are known: which songs are in it and which are not
No order and no repeats: a second "Wave" is not added to the set
In a playlist one song can appear twice, in a set it cannot
The order in the playlist changed — the set of songs is the same

body.text: In code this is the difference between an array and a set: a list remembers order and repeats, a set only membership.

slides.title: Equality and the empty set
slides.sub: The same elements — so they are equal
slides.main: A set remembers only its contents: the order of writing and repeats change nothing.

captions: Two notations, one with a repeat: {1, 2} and {2, 1, 1}
Repeats and order change nothing — it is the same set
A special inhabitant is the empty set: it has no elements at all
There is only one: the sum over nothing is zero, a search finds nothing

body.text: Like the empty set of a freshly created object: convenient when emptiness looks the same everywhere.

slides.title: Three operations
slides.main: Almost any problem about lists of people or products comes down to a combination of them.

captions: A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6}: the common elements 3 and 4 are in both
The sets approach each other…
The common elements merged: in a set each value appears once
A ∪ B = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 } — everything that is in at least one set
A ∩ B = { 3, 4 } — only what is in both
A \ B = { 1, 2 } — A without what is in B

body.text: You already know them under other names: merging sets, a union query in a database, intersecting friend lists.

slides.title: Complement and universe
slides.main: A complement is "everything that did not pass the filter", but only inside the chosen universe.

captions: The fourth operation is the complement: first we must agree on what to count from
The universe U is all the elements we are considering at all
The complement of administrators A is all the other users
We changed the universe to the people of the planet — the complement became different, but A is the same
In code this is "everything that did not pass the filter"

body.text: Change the universe from users to the people on the planet — and the complement becomes different, even though the set A itself has not changed.

slides.title: De Morgan's laws
slides.main: It is not true that at least one of the two holds — so neither of them holds.

captions: The operations obey laws; the most famous are De Morgan's laws
First: the complement of a union is everything outside both circles, that is ¬A ∩ ¬B
Second: the complement of an intersection is everything except the common part, that is ¬A ∪ ¬B
Why: an element outside the union is in neither A nor B — so it is in both complements
A shop: "not cheap and not old" is the same as "not (cheap or old)"
A task is accepted if the tests are green and the review has passed; not accepted if at least one is violated
A common mistake: "not admin or not editor" lets almost everyone through
Correct: "not admin and not editor" — or "not" of a bracket with "or"
In code and in a database it is the same: negation flips "or" and "and"
Negation flips "or" into "and" and back

frames.text: not (cheap or old) = not cheap and not old
not (tests and review) = red tests or no review
¬A ∪ ¬B: everyone except those who are both admin and editor
not admin AND not editor = not (admin or editor)
= WHERE NOT a AND NOT b

body.text: You don't need to memorize these laws like a spell — it is enough to feel once that negation flips "or" into "and" and back.

slides.title: Cardinality and double counting
slides.sub: Size of a set, length of an array, number of records
slides.main: The cardinality of a union is rarely equal to the sum of the cardinalities: sets overlap.

captions: Cardinality |A| is the number of elements: like the size of an array or the number of records in a query
20 people know English and 20 know German: naively add and get 40
But those who know both languages appeared in both lists — in a union they are counted once
The honest count is the inclusion–exclusion formula: a separate chapter is devoted to it
Naive addition is the classic double-counting mistake

body.text: How to count honestly over overlapping sets — we will work out in the chapter on inclusion and exclusion.

slides.title: Subsets
slides.sub: Each element of the smaller one also belongs to the larger one
slides.main: Checking a subset comes down to an intersection: A ⊆ B if A ∩ B = A.

captions: If every element of A is also in B, then A is a subset of B: A ⊆ B
Even numbers are a subset of the integers: every even number is an integer
The editor's permissions are a subset of the administrator's: without configuring the system
Check: the intersection with the larger set coincided with the smaller one — it is nested

body.text: If the intersection of the smaller set with the larger coincided with the smaller, it is nested: A ⊆ B when A ∩ B = A.

slides.title: Power set: 2ⁿ subsets
slides.sub: The set of all subsets of the original
slides.main: For each element there are two choices — take it or not, so there are exactly 2ⁿ subsets.

captions: The power set is the set of all subsets of the original set
If a set has n elements, the power set has 2ⁿ subsets
For each element — two choices: take or not, 2 · 2 · 2 decisions in all
Three elements — eight subsets, ten — already one thousand and twenty-four
A bit mask: one bit per element, every number is a ready-made subset

body.text: When building a subset you decide for each element: take it or not — two choices for each of the n elements.

slides.title: The price of brute force
slides.sub: The exponential is the most expensive operation of the course
slides.main: If you see 2ⁿ in a solution — stop and think: it is your time budget.

captions: Going through all subsets grows exponentially — it is the most expensive operation of the course
Already at thirty elements there are more than a billion options
That is why discrete mathematics treasures every chance not to enumerate but to calculate with a formula
Two to the power of n is your time budget: if you see it in a solution — stop

frames.text: n = 30: more than a billion options
formula: we count, not enumerate — instantly

body.text: "Split the load into two groups as evenly as possible" is most honestly solved by going through subsets — that is why discrete mathematics treasures every chance to use a formula.

slides.title: Sets at work
slides.main: When you think in sets, the code gets shorter: instead of a loop with a flag — one intersection operation.

captions: Let's see where this lives in everyday work: here is a list of values with repeats
A membership check in a hash set costs a constant: deduplication is simply converting a list into a set
In SQL the same operations are UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT — and the database runs them on millions of rows
Analytics filters, user segments, article tags — under the hood there are sets and intersections
When you think in sets, instead of a loop with a flag — one intersection operation

frames.text: one operation instead of a loop

body.text: All of this is the same operations under different names in different tools.

slides.title: List or set
slides.main: A bad sign is a list that you search through inside a loop: almost always it is a set disguised as a list.

captions: A list and a set are different contracts under similar syntax
A list keeps order and allows repeats: a task queue, a history, paginated output
A set keeps the fact of membership and instantly answers "is there one of these here"
Searching inside a list in a loop means going through all the elements one by one
If you search in a list — it is almost always a set disguised as a list

body.text: Choosing the right structure is half of an algorithm, and sets give you that half for free.

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: Sets and database queries now have a precise language.

captions: Summing up the chapter
A set is elements without order and repeats
Operations: union, intersection, difference and complement
De Morgan's laws link negation with these operations
Cardinality counts the elements
The power set contains 2ⁿ subsets
You have already used all of this in sets and database queries — now the tools have a precise language
Next — relations and functions: foreign keys, table links, pure functions

body.text: The next chapter is relations and functions: foreign keys, table links and the pure functions you write every day.
